nuance: 인터넷 is the plain loanword (from English 'internet') for the network itself, and 'to go online' is normally 인터넷을 하다 — Korean turns the bare noun into an activity with 하다 rather than coining a separate verb. Do not confuse it with 와이파이 (the local wireless signal you connect to) or 데이터 (your phone's mobile data plan): you can have 인터넷 through either. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you search 인터넷으로 (by means of the internet), never 인터넷에 — 에 would wrongly treat the internet as a static location. Also, when it stops working Koreans say 인터넷이 안 돼요 (it doesn't function), not 인터넷이 없어요, which would mean the service literally doesn't exist there.

nuance: 비밀번호 is Sino-Korean: 秘密 (비밀, 'secret') + 番號 (번호, 'number/code'), literally a 'secret number', so it naturally covers PINs and door-lock codes as well as login passwords. In casual speech almost everyone clips it to 비번, which is fine among friends but too slangy for a written form or a bank's formal prompt. The nearest neighbour is 암호 (暗號), which leans toward a cipher, secret signal, or military-style code; 비밀번호 is the ordinary everyday word you'll see on every signup screen. A common English-speaker slip is to assume you 'know' a password and reach for 알다, but for the action of typing it Korean prefers 입력하다 or 넣다 with the object marker: 비밀번호를 입력하다. When it's mistyped, say 비밀번호가 틀리다 (it's incorrect), not 비밀번호가 나쁘다.

Note the gentle contrast with 프로그램, which Koreans tend to use for desktop/PC software, while 앱 implies the phone. nuance: 검색 is Sino-Korean: 檢 (검, 'inspect/examine') + 索 (색, 'search/seek out'), so it's the act of looking information up, especially online, and it readily becomes the verb 검색하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the recipient is marked with 한테/에게 ('to a person'), not the English bare object — 친구한테 메시지를 보내다, where 친구한테 = 'to my friend' and 메시지를 is the thing sent; second, the message arriving uses intransitive 오다 with 이/가 (메시지가 오다), but you sending it uses 보내다 with 을/를 (메시지를 보내다). Don't carry the English 'send him a message' double-object pattern straight over.

structuredNuance.t: 메시지 is the loanword from English 'message' and covers chat/app messages broadly (a KakaoTalk message, a DM).

The everyday near-synonym 문자 (literally 文字 'letters/characters') specifically means an SMS text, so '문자 보내' = 'text me' while '메시지' is the wider term. There's also 카톡, the verb-able brand shorthand for a KakaoTalk message, used constantly in real life (카톡 보낼게 'I'll Kakao you').

mistakes: Saying 메시지가 보내요 for 'I send a message'. 보내다 is transitive: 메시지를 보내요.
Marking the recipient with the object marker, e.g. 친구를 메시지를 보내요. The person who receives it takes 한테/에게: 친구한테 메시지를 보내요.
Treating 메시지 and 문자 as identical. 문자 specifically means an SMS text; for that, '문자 보낼게' is the natural phrase, while 메시지 is the broader word for any app message.

examples: I write text with the keyboard.
으로 = the tool; 글을 = the object written
subject 이 with the adjective 편하다
nuance: 키보드 is the loanword for a computer or on-screen typing keyboard; note that a piano-style musical keyboard is also called 키보드, but the bank of keys themselves is 건반 and the Korean character layout is the 자판. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the right verb-particle pair: when the keyboard is the tool you write with, use 으로 (키보드로 쓰다), but when you focus on striking the keys, Korean uses 치다 ('to hit/strike') with the object marker — 키보드를 치다 — the same 치다 used for 피아노를 치다 'play piano' and 타자를 치다 'type'. So 'typing' as an action is most idiomatically 타자를 치다 or 키보드를 치다, while 쓰다 emphasizes the text produced. Don't use 에 with the keyboard (키보드에 써요 is wrong for the instrument); 에 would mark a surface you write onto, like 종이에 쓰다 'write on paper'.

Saying 키보드가 쳐요 for tapping the keys. 치다 is transitive: 키보드를 쳐요.
